title: FOGLINE update: I deleted the action economy, and the submarine is now a probability cloud (serious game built with Claude, single HTML file)
author: DueSpkyke
selftext:
A while back I posted about wanting a serious game less depressing than DEFCON. Short recap: FOGLINE is a browser strategy game about deciding under uncertainty. Real maps, fictional crises. You get evidence, competing hypotheses and a clock, and the debrief shows what was actually true.

It is still one HTML file (about 9 MB, no backend), still written almost entirely with Claude. Here is what changed since then, and what I learned about working this way.

\*\*What changed in the game\*\*

\- \*\*Fewer, sharper missions.\*\* I cut the catalogue from 75 scenarios to 9 missions, one theme each, across six real theatres: port cyberattack, seabed cables, sub hunt, naval escalation, tanker seizure, drone swarm, evacuation, mines, and a humanitarian convoy where losing half the ships triggers its own crisis.

\- \*\*No more action tokens.\*\* Every action used to cost a token per turn. It made the game feel like accounting. They are gone. What limits you now is time, authorization delays, fuel and stock.

\- \*\*Slower and longer.\*\* One slow speed for every unit, missions of 22 to 31 turns. You have time to read before you decide.

\- \*\*The submarine is no longer a circle.\*\* The contact used to be a search circle that quietly re-centred on the true position. Now it is a probability grid. Every sensor reshapes it, including the ones that hear nothing. Silence empties the area they cover.

\- \*\*You have to earn the shot.\*\* A torpedo is only offered when the estimate is tight enough, the "submarine" hypothesis is strong enough and the last measurement is fresh. Otherwise the button stays visible and tells you what is missing.

\- \*\*Crisis window.\*\* Each new crisis opens a short illustrated brief with facts, hypotheses and possible responses, and the clock stops while you read.

\*\*What I learned about building this with an AI\*\*

1. \*\*Bots before opinions.\*\* Every version is played by scripted players: a reference player, an omniscient one that reads the truth, one that gives no orders, one that shoots without checking. If "no orders" wins a mission, the mission is broken. That check caught two missions you could win by doing nothing.

2. \*\*One list of legal actions.\*\* The UI and the bots read the same function. No button exists that the tests cannot press, and no test uses a shortcut the player does not have.

3. \*\*Same seed, same game.\*\* Everything random in the engine goes through one generator. It is the only reason I can compare two versions at all.

4. \*\*A long instruction file that records decisions.\*\* Not just rules: what was decided, when, by whom, and what was \*not\* verified. The model stops re-arguing settled choices and stops overclaiming.

5. \*\*Removing things was the hard part.\*\* Deleting tokens touched scoring, the HUD, about twenty test files and all the balance numbers. The AI is fast at adding. Taking something out cleanly needed much more of my attention.

\*\*What I do not know\*\*

\- No real player has tested any of this. Every number I have comes from scripts.

\- The reference bot now wins about 78% of games. My target was 50 to 70%, so it is probably too easy since I removed the limits.

\- Bots do not feel time pressure. They say nothing about whether it is fun or whether anyone learns something.

\- Scores and gauges are game models, not measurements of anything.

\*\*Links\*\*

\- Playable build: [https://otakuch.github.io/fogline/](https://otakuch.github.io/fogline/)

\- Source: [https://github.com/otakuch/fogline](https://github.com/otakuch/fogline)

\- 54-second video with a sub hunt example.

I am looking for people willing to play one mission and tell me where they got lost. The sub hunt ("Deep-water hunt") is the one I most need eyes on. Ten minutes and a blunt comment would help more than another thousand bot runs.

comments.author: TailorGame
comments.body: Cutting from 75 scenarios to 9 sharper missions sounds like the right call, especially for a game about deciding under uncertainty where every scenario has to teach something. Keeping it in a single HTML file written with Claude is impressive. One suggestion for that workflow is to keep a short design doc of the rules and scoring model that you paste in each session, so the model doesn't quietly drift the mechanics while it refactors.
